# The Taste Gym — full description for AI readers

## What it is

The Taste Gym is a web product that measures and trains musical taste against the five criteria
David Hume laid out in "Of the Standard of Taste" (1757): delicacy of taste, practice, comparison,
freedom from prejudice, and good sense. It is an evaluation product, not a prediction product: it
never predicts personality, mood, or psychological states, and it never scores taste by
self-report. Every instrument is a performance task where the user can be objectively wrong, and
every score is computed by a deterministic engine in code — no machine-learning model or language
model classifies the user.

The product is free, and there is no paid tier and no pricing question: the assessment, the
headline score, and the training arc when it exists are all free. The only gate is a seven-day
per-family retest cooldown, which exists because a retest taken sooner measures a person's memory
of the clips rather than their ear. It is a validity gate, not a revenue gate.

## The Prestige Test (flagship instrument, live)

The Prestige Test measures Hume's "freedom from prejudice" criterion as a number.

Design: a within-subject experiment taking about eight minutes. The user rates sixteen short music
clips blind (no labels), then rates the same clips again — fourteen with artist names and
prestige framing attached, and two clips carry no label in either pass (drift controls). Two of
the fourteen labels are deliberately false — a modest work presented with borrowed acclaim, or a
distinguished one presented as unknown. Because the user rates the same audio twice, they serve
as their own control: the component of rating movement that tracks the labels (including the
false ones) can only be explained by prestige, not by the music. The unlabeled control clips
measure each user's plain second-pass drift (memory, familiarity, regression), and the headline
subtracts the residual that drift would leave in the sway statistic. The headline result is the
drift-corrected share of rating movement that flowed toward the labels.

The deception is disclosed: the test ends with a mandatory debrief screen that names every swapped
label, gives the true attribution, and shows what the user's ratings did under each false name.
There is no path around the debrief.

All audio is public-domain or Creative-Commons licensed, with attribution and license recorded per
item. The item pool is versioned; every stored response and share link carries the pool version so
data remains interpretable when items change.

## The Delicacy Trials (second instrument, live)

Hume's "delicacy" criterion, after the key-in-the-wine story Hume borrows from Don Quixote:
public-domain/CC recordings are processed with controlled degradations — pitch drift, timing
smear, and lossy-codec artifacts — and the user hears each pair and says which member is damaged,
then names the flaw. A session is three practice trials with the answer shown immediately,
followed by fifteen scored pairs.

The readout is a detection band, not a rank. Because a two-alternative choice can be won by
guessing, the score is guessing-corrected and reported as an interval (a Wilson interval on the
corrected rate) rather than a point. At this session length it takes twelve of fifteen to beat the
coin at 95% confidence, and the readout says so. Six ranked tiers shipped here until August 2026
and were deleted: measured against simulated respondents they placed a person in the correct tier
30.5% of the time, and no coarser cut rescued them.

On performance items the user attaches a confidence level (95% / 70% / 50%) to each answer;
confidence-versus-accuracy yields a calibration curve and Brier score, which operationalizes
Hume's "good sense" criterion. Confidence never weights or inflates scores — it is measured
against accuracy, never blended in.

## The Threshold Test (third instrument, live)

Delicacy measured as a size rather than a count. An adaptive staircase makes the damage smaller
after each correct answer and larger after each miss, converging on the smallest flaw the listener
can still detect. It runs one flaw family per session and reports that family's threshold in
physical units: cents of peak detune for pitch drift, milliseconds of drift IQR for timing smear,
and kbps for lossy-codec artifacts. The deliverable is a per-flaw sensitivity threshold in real
units, not a score.

The instrument publishes what it cannot do. Ladder rungs that are not acoustically separable,
levels whose damage varies by passage, and the floor of what the rulers can report are measured by
the clip pipeline and listed at /lab/instrument-limits in the pipeline's own words.

## Comparison (no instrument yet)

Hume's "comparison" criterion is breadth of exposure — a fact about listening history rather than
a testable skill. It is in the plan and not in the product. What it waits on is a decision about
what breadth means in units the product can defend, not an audio build; the reading-room page for
comparison says this plainly rather than implying a door that is not there. The same is true of
practice, which waits on the product remembering a person between sessions, which it does not
do today.

## Methodology and honesty rules

1. Performance tasks over self-report: every score derives from what the user did on a task, not
   what they said about themselves.
2. Within-subject control: blind-vs-labeled and baseline-vs-retest comparisons remove the need for
   external ground truth about musical quality.
3. Deterministic scoring in code: same responses, same score, always; scoring rules are
   inspectable. Where AI writes narrative, it narrates an already-computed number and cannot
   change it.
4. No number the data can't back: until a real calibration cohort exists, all results are labeled
   provisional and no percentiles are shown anywhere. Published statistics state their N. The
   psychometrics pipeline uses item-response theory, signal-detection analysis, calibration/Brier
   analysis, and reliability checks before any norm is published.

Data collected: anonymized response vectors only — ratings, per-item listen durations, item-pool
version, and computed scores under a random per-session id. No accounts, no names, no emails, no
ad-tech cookies.
